title: Referrals and repeat work from existing clients for Mobile beauty
audience: Solo mobile beauty therapists who want repeat treatments and referrals from clients they have already seen at home.
learningOutcomes: Plan a review or referral request that is made after the client has judged the result, and that the client can decline easily
Write a next-treatment offer with a date, a scope and a price approach, and schedule the check-in that follows it
Write referral reward terms, including the payment condition, before any referral is made

instruction.heading: Ask once the client has judged the result
instruction.body: The best time to ask for a review or referral is after the client has confirmed that the treatment is right, or when the visit is paid. Ask in one sentence, name the step you would like, such as a review or the name of one person who might want a treatment, and make it easy to decline. Record what you asked and what the client said. Timing matters, but the evidence is thin. The AMA (10 January 2023) says timing should match the product type, because experience goods need more time to evaluate than search goods, and a facial or a manicure is closer to an experience good. In one Baylor Keller Center experiment, a late reminder brought in more reviews than an immediate one, with 1.32 per cent reviewing without a reminder and 2.16 per cent with a late reminder. That is one experiment, not a beauty study. Sending a review link or QR code is allowed, and Google provides one. Do not write reviews for clients or invent them. Do not ask only the happy clients, because Podium, a review software vendor, says Google treats that as a violation. Google bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews, and the ACCC says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on what the review says.

instruction.heading: Offer the next treatment before the client leaves
instruction.body: Repeat treatments are the most useful work for a mobile beauty therapist to plan. Before the client leaves, propose the next treatment with a date, the scope, the interval and the price approach, and write it down. The research gives no interval for beauty, so choose one and test it against your own bookings. Confirm that the client agrees before you change their schedule. If the offer goes by email or text, check the electronic message rules first. The ACMA’s guidance says inferred consent is narrow and does not cover a message sent just after a purchase.

instruction.heading: Check in at an interval you test
instruction.body: Schedule a short check-in after a period that suits the treatment, and record the answer. The check asks whether the result still holds, whether anything has changed and whether a further treatment is wanted. A check-in that only asks about the result may not be commercial, but a message that promotes a service can be, even when framed as a reminder. ACMA’s summary does not say whether one-to-one messages are covered, so check that point before you send. For context only, a vendor survey of UK and Irish salon guests reported that 29 per cent of new clients rebook (Phorest, 2025). That is salon data from outside Australia, not mobile data.

instruction.heading: Re-contact previous clients before their busy periods
instruction.body: Plan a short message before any period you can see in your own booking records, such as a seasonal peak. The research found no source for beauty demand peaks, so the periods must come from your records. Offer the times you can deliver, on written terms, with a clear way to opt out. Do not use the message to pressure anyone. ACMA’s guidance says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days, so record each opt-out when you receive it and stop sending to that client.

instruction.heading: Set referral rewards in writing before anyone refers
instruction.body: A referral reward works best when the client knows the terms before they refer someone. Decide what you will offer, such as a credit on the next treatment, and write down the condition for payment, normally that the referred person has completed a paid treatment. Tell the referrer the terms, keep a record of each referral and whether the reward was paid, and never promise a reward you cannot deliver. A study of referral programmes in seven experiments found that stating the referrer’s reward in the invitation increased referrals, so say what the reward is in the invitation. Get the referred person’s consent before any referral message is sent. The tax and contract effect of a credit or cash reward is not confirmed by any source read, so check it with an adviser.

procedure: After each treatment is complete and the client has confirmed the result, make one review or referral request and record what was asked and the answer.
Write the next-treatment offer with a date, scope, interval and price approach, and confirm it with the client.
Schedule the check-in at an interval you have chosen and can test, and send it using the electronic message rules.
Plan a re-contact message for each period shown in your booking records, and exclude anyone who has opted out.
Write the referral reward terms and the payment condition before the first referral is made.
When a referral books and is paid, apply the reward and record the outcome.
Review at the end of each season which requests, offers and timings produced repeat treatments.

workedExamples.situation: A mobile beauty therapist finishes a facial for a regular client. The client says she will recommend the therapist to her sister, who lives in the same street. The therapist wants to offer a credit on her next treatment if the sister books.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the therapist do before the sister books, and what should she avoid?
workedExamples.reasoning: She writes down the reward terms before any referral happens: the credit, the condition that the sister completes a paid treatment, and when the credit will be applied. She asks her client to pass on the sister’s details, and she contacts the sister only if the sister agrees. She does not promise a reward she has not written down. If she is unsure of the tax or contract effect of the credit, she confirms it with an adviser. She books no treatment that her qualifications, registration and insurance do not cover in the state where the visit happens.

equipmentAndPpe: Client record with the treatment date, the sign-off and the review or referral request made
Next-treatment offer template with scope, interval and price approach
Calendar of re-contact dates taken from your own booking records
No PPE is needed for client follow-up; any home visit follows the client’s own access rules and your own hygiene routine

commonErrors.error: Asking for a review before the client has judged the result.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask after the client has confirmed the treatment is right, or after payment, and make it easy to decline.

commonErrors.error: Offering a referral reward that was never written down, so the terms are disputed later.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the reward and its payment condition before any referral is made, and give the referrer a copy.

commonErrors.error: Publishing a client’s name, photo or review without their consent for that use.
commonErrors.prevention: Get consent for each thing you plan to publish, and keep the record.

commonErrors.error: Contacting a client who asked not to hear from you, or using a re-contact message to pressure them.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep an opt-out list, honour it at once, and keep re-contact messages factual and optional.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Publishing a client’s name, photo, review or home address needs the client’s consent for that use. Do not write reviews on a client’s behalf or invent them. If the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business, client details are personal information. The research did not confirm whether it applies to a small business, so check the OAIC’s small business guidance.

Review platforms and referral programmes can have their own rules on incentives. Google bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews. The ACCC’s guidance on online reviews says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on the review’s content. Check each platform’s rules before offering any reward.

Check-in and re-contact messages sent by email or text can be commercial electronic messages under the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). A message that promotes a service can be commercial even when it is framed as a service reminder, so check each message before sending. The Act text itself was not read.

A referral does not extend the licence, registration or authority of the therapist who accepts the work. Accept only the treatments your qualifications, registration and insurance cover, in the state where the treatment is given. In Queensland, higher-risk skin-penetration services need a licence. In the Northern Territory, a business paid for beauty therapy must register. Rules differ between states and territories. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Every review or referral request is made after the client has confirmed the result, and it includes an easy way to decline.
Every next-treatment offer is written, has a date and is confirmed by the client before the schedule changes.
Every referral reward has written terms and a payment condition, and is paid only when that condition is met.
documentationEvidence: Review or referral request log with the date sent and the answer.
Next-treatment offers with the date, scope, interval and client confirmation.
Referral reward terms with the referral record and payment outcome.
summary: Ask for reviews and referrals after the client has confirmed the result, and make it easy to say no.
Offer the next treatment in writing, with a date, before the client leaves.
Set referral rewards and their payment conditions in writing before anyone refers.

knowledgeChecks.question: When is the best time to ask a client for a review or referral?
options: Before the treatment starts, so the client feels committed
After the client has confirmed the result is right
Only when the client has sent you a complaint

knowledgeChecks.question: A client wants to publish a review with their name and a photo of the finished treatment. What do you need?
options: Their consent for the name and photo you plan to publish
Nothing, because the review is positive
Your own judgement that the photo looks professional

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a referral reward look like?
options: Paid to anyone who mentions your name
Decided after the referred person books, based on how keen the referrer seems
Decided and written in advance, with the condition for payment stated

knowledgeChecks.question: When does the lesson say to propose the next treatment for the client?
options: At the end of each visit, with a date

sourceReferences: Team 4 repeat and referral research (/home/claude/tasks/team4-R-repeat-referral-tactics.md) and personal-services research for beauty (/home/claude/tasks/team4-V-personal-services-a.md), both 2026-11-09. Only sources read in those files are listed.

Baylor Keller Center, 'Wait Just a Minute', https://kellercenter.hankamer.baylor.edu/news/story/2024/wait-just-minute-when-ask-online-reviews, 1 June 2024 (metadata says 13 May 2024). One experiment only.

AMA, 'Asking for customer reviews at the right time', https://www.ama.org/2023/01/10/asking-for-customer-reviews-at-the-right-time-sooner-is-not-always-better/, 10 January 2023. Supports: timing should match the product type.
Podium, 'Review gating', https://www.podium.com/article/review-gating, 2 May 2022. Vendor source; the Google position it describes was not checked against Google’s policy.

ACCC, 'Online reviews for product and services', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/advertising-and-promotions/online-reviews-for-product-and-services, published and updated 15 July 2026. Supports: incentives disclosed and not dependent on review content.

Xu, Yu and Tu, Journal of Marketing Research 60(2), 2023, https://research.polyu.edu.hk/en/publications/i-will-get-a-reward-too-when-disclosing-the-referrer-reward-incre/. Supports: stating the reward in the invitation increased referrals; general consumer studies, no figures used.

Clayton Utz, 'Referrer beware', https://www.claytonutz.com/insights/2017/may/referrer-beware-proceed-with-caution-when-contemplating-refer-a-friend-promotions, 11 May 2017 (older than 2022). Supports: referred person’s consent.
ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam', https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, no date shown. Supports: consent, sender identity, unsubscribe honoured within five working days; inferred consent is narrow.

Clayton Utz, 'The ACMA cranks up enforcement', https://www.claytonutz.com/insights/2023/november/the-acma-cranks-up-enforcement-do-your-factual-customer-emails-pass-the-spam-act-test, 9 November 2023. Supports: a factual reminder that promotes a service can be commercial.

Phorest Consumer Insights Report 2025, as reported by Professional Beauty, https://professionalbeauty.co.uk/only-29-percent-new-salon-clients-rebook-phorest-research, 18 August 2025, updated 15 September 2025. Vendor data; 716 UK and Irish salon guests; 29 per cent of new clients rebook. Not Australian or mobile.

Nielsen, 'Earned advertising remains most credible among consumers', https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2013/nielsen-earned-advertising-remains-most-credible-among-consumer/, September 2013. Older than 2022; general survey, not beauty evidence.

Gaps: no business.gov.au or ACCC guidance on referral rewards; no mobile beauty source on referral or venue partnerships; no interval for repeat treatments in beauty; Support at Home and NDIS do not name beauty in the parts checked.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Says commercial messages need the recipient’s consent, must identify the sender and carry an unsubscribe option honoured within five working days. Does not mention one-to-one messages. Publisher: ACMA.
